title.title: Interoperability
title.subtitle: Why many chains need to talk — bridges, Cosmos IBC, Layer 0, and XRP

layer0Anim.headline: A tx travelling L2 → L1 → L0 → L1 → L2
steps: 1. L2 rollup posts a batch back to L1 (settlement)
2. L1 sends a cross-chain message through the Layer 0 hub
3. Layer 0 relays it to a different L1 (XCM / Warp / IBC)
4. Destination L1 delivers it down to its own L2

xrplAxelarAnim.headline: XRPL → Axelar → another blockchain
steps: 1. User triggers a cross-chain call from XRPL (e.g. send RLUSD to Ethereum)
2. Axelar gateway picks up the message; validators vote on the payload
3. ≥ 2/3 of Axelar validators sign — the message is admitted on the hub
4. Axelar relayer delivers to the destination chain; recipient receives it

interop.heading: Why do blockchains need to talk to each other?
interop.subtitle: Every chain you have met so far keeps its own ledger, its own money and its own rules. None of them can read the others — by design.
interop.recap: Bitcoin (Section 01) · Ethereum (Section 02) · Hyperledger Fabric (Section 03) — each one is its own island
interop.analogy: Early email: a Gmail user could not write to a Hotmail user until providers agreed on a shared standard. Blockchains today are mostly still at the "no shared standard" stage.

svg.caption: Each island validates only its own ledger. A coin cannot "swim" across.

islands.title: Three problems that follow
islands.intro: Islands are fine until value and users want to move. Then three frictions appear:

cards.title: Stranded assets
cards.desc: Bitcoin cannot be used inside an Ethereum app. To get it there, someone has to hold the real BTC and issue an IOU (WBTC) — so you now trust that someone.

cards.title: Fragile connections
cards.desc: The connectors built so far (bridges) have lost more money than any other part of crypto — Ronin $625M, Wormhole $320M, Nomad $190M.

cards.title: Split-up markets
cards.desc: Every chain has its own exchanges and pools. The same token can trade at different prices on different chains, and moving between them costs time and fees.

matters.title: Why It Matters
matters.intro: True interoperability unlocks a multi-chain world where assets and messages flow freely:
items: Pay with BTC inside an Ethereum DeFi protocol — trustlessly
Transfer an NFT from Ethereum to Solana while keeping provenance
An enterprise Hyperledger Fabric network settling final state on Ethereum
A single user interface accessing liquidity across 10 chains simultaneously
matters.solutionsLabel: Three ways to connect — compared in two slides

solutions.label: Layer 0
solutions.sub: One security team for many chains

usecases.heading: Where this shows up in real life
usecases.subtitle: Interoperability sounds abstract until you see who needs it. Six everyday situations — and how value crosses today.

items.title: Moving to a cheaper lane
items.scenario: You hold ETH on Ethereum, but a swap costs $20 in fees. You move it to Arbitrum or Base, where the same swap costs cents.

items.title: Using Bitcoin in DeFi
items.scenario: You want to earn yield on BTC inside an Ethereum lending app. A custodian holds the BTC and issues WBTC you can use.

items.title: One stablecoin, many chains
items.scenario: USDC lives natively on a dozen-plus chains; Circle's CCTP burns it on one chain and mints it on another. RLUSD settles on XRPL and Ethereum.

items.title: Game items that travel
items.scenario: A game runs on its own chain for speed (Ronin, Immutable), but players want to sell items on an Ethereum marketplace.

items.title: Private data, public settlement
items.scenario: A consortium keeps supplier data on a private Fabric network but wants final settlement or tokens on a public chain for liquidity.

items.title: Cross-border payment routes
items.scenario: A payment starts as a stablecoin on one chain and must arrive as a local-currency token on another — in one trip, not three hops.

usecases.footer: in every case somebody has to hold the asset or verify the other chain. Who that is — an operator, the maths, or a shared validator set — is the whole design question. Next slide.

interopCompare.heading: Three ways to connect chains
interopCompare.subtitle: Same question each time — who do you have to trust for the hand-over? Read the analogy row first; the rest is detail.

col1.title: Bridges & Wrapped Tokens
col1.subtitle: Lock-and-mint · an operator in the middle
col1.analogy: A courier keeps your luggage and gives you a claim ticket to use in the other city.
col1.mechanism: Your coin is locked in a vault on chain A; a copy ("wrapped" token) is issued on chain B. Burn the copy to get the original back.
col1.trust: The bridge operators — usually a small group of signers who approve every release.
col1.risk: The vault holds everyone's coins in one place. If the signers' keys leak or the code has a bug, the whole vault goes.
col1.finality: Minutes to hours depending on source-chain confirmation depth
col1.compatibility: Works between any two chains with no shared infrastructure required
col1.examples: WBTC · Ronin · Wormhole · Hop Protocol · LayerZero · Stargate

col2.title: Protocol-native / IBC
col2.subtitle: Chains verify each other directly
col2.analogy: Both airports read each other's boarding passes directly — no courier needed.
col2.mechanism: Each chain keeps a tiny copy of the other's block headers and checks the proof itself. Messages travel; coins are escrowed per connection, not in one giant vault.
col2.trust: The maths and the two chains' own validators — no extra company or committee.
col2.risk: Only as strong as the weaker of the two chains. Both must speak the same standard, which limits reach today.
col2.finality: As fast as both chains' consensus — typically 1–6 seconds end-to-end
col2.compatibility: Requires both chains to implement the IBC standard — limited to the IBC ecosystem today
col2.examples: Cosmos IBC (110+ chains) · IBC Eureka (Ethereum) · Polkadot XCM (within parachains)

col3.title: Layer 0 Network
col3.subtitle: One security team for many chains
col3.analogy: One security team guards every terminal in the airport — moving between terminals is just walking.
col3.mechanism: A shared validator set secures all connected chains at once, so sending a message between them is a built-in operation, not a separate contract.
col3.trust: The Layer 0's validators — the same people who finalise blocks also carry the messages.
col3.risk: Everything inside is as safe as the Layer 0 itself. To reach chains outside the club you still need a bridge.
col3.finality: Native — cross-chain calls settle in the same block production cycle as regular transactions
col3.compatibility: Chains must plug into the L0 and conform to its runtime rules — maximum security, minimum flexibility
col3.examples: Polkadot (Relay Chain + XCM) · Avalanche (Primary Network + Warp) · Babylon (BTC security layer)

layer0.heading: Layer 0 — The Substrate Beneath the L1s
layer0.leadStrong: validators, security, and a messaging fabric
layer0.leadB: to many L1s at once — and the cross-chain call you saw in
layer0.leadC: is a native protocol operation, not a bridge contract.
layer0.inOneLine: Internet backbone analogy: many ISPs (L1s) plug into shared cables (L0) instead of each laying their own.

provides.title: Shared security
provides.desc: A pooled validator set secures every L1 connected to it. New chains inherit security on day 1.

provides.title: Native cross-chain messaging
provides.desc: L0 defines the message format and trust model (XCM, Warp) — no third-party bridge needed.

provides.title: Shared infrastructure
provides.desc: Block production, finality, governance and upgrades live at L0. L1s focus on application logic.

layer02.subtitle: The three active L0 networks today — and how the L0 model compares to Cosmos's sovereign-chain approach.

bridges.heading: Bridges — useful, and the most hacked thing in crypto
bridges.subA: Bridges are the plumbing that makes a multi-chain world usable. They are also the most exploited component: roughly
bridges.subB: was stolen from bridges in 2022 alone — about two-thirds of everything stolen in crypto that year.

vault.label: How a lock-and-mint bridge works
vault.caption: Every user adds to the same vault. The bigger it gets, the bigger the prize — that is the honeypot.

bridges.honest: Using a bridge is a trust decision, not a technical detail: you are trusting whoever controls the vault. Prefer a chain's official (canonical) bridge, and move only what you need.

hacks.name: Ronin Bridge
hacks.method: 5 of the 9 signer keys were stolen — enough to approve any withdrawal from the vault.

hacks.name: Wormhole Bridge
hacks.method: A signature check could be skipped — the attacker issued 120,000 wrapped ETH backed by nothing.

hacks.name: Nomad Bridge
hacks.method: A setup mistake made every message look valid. Hundreds of copycats emptied it within hours.

hacks.name: Harmony Horizon
hacks.method: Only 2 of 5 signers were needed — two stolen keys were enough.

dangers.title: One vault, everyone's coins
dangers.desc: The locked assets sit in a single contract. A bridge holding $500M is a $500M prize for whoever finds a bug.

dangers.title: A few people hold the keys
dangers.desc: Most bridges release funds when a small group of signers agree. Steal enough keys and the vault is yours.

dangers.title: Two chains, twice the complexity
dangers.desc: The bridge must understand both chains at once — different rules, timings and signature formats. More surface, more bugs.

dangers.title: Finality Mismatch
dangers.desc: Optimistic bridges release funds before finality is confirmed on the source chain. If a transaction is later reorganized (reorged), the bridge may have already minted assets on the destination with no backing.

safer.title: Chains verify each other (IBC)
safer.desc: No operator, no single vault — each chain checks the other's proofs. No known loss of funds from an IBC-protocol exploit so far.

safer.title: Official (canonical) bridges
safer.desc: Ethereum rollups' own bridges (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base) are secured by the rollup's proof system, not by a separate group of signers.

safer.title: Large Multisig Thresholds
safer.desc: 5-of-9 is the minimum acceptable. Ronin used 5-of-9 but had only 4 real signers. Hardware security modules (HSMs) for key storage are mandatory.

safer.title: Formal Verification
safer.desc: Message passing logic and signature verification code should be formally verified — not just audited. Wormhole's bug passed manual audit.

safer.title: Rate limits & circuit breakers
safer.desc: Cap how much can leave per hour. Nomad was drained in minutes — a limit would have saved most of it.

cosmos.heading: Cosmos: The Internet of Blockchains
cosmos.subtitle: A network of sovereign, interoperable chains connected by the IBC protocol — each one optimised for its specific use case.
cosmos.pill1Text: — IBC is the native protocol, not a bridge bolted on top
cosmos.pill2Text: — every zone is a purpose-built chain (DEX, perps, GPU compute…)
cosmos.archNote: Zones can also IBC each other directly (mesh)

properties.title: IBC Protocol
properties.desc: Inter-Blockchain Communication — TCP/IP for blockchains. Light-client verification on each side; trustless messaging and asset transfer between any IBC-enabled chain.

properties.title: Cosmos SDK
properties.desc: Go framework to build app-specific chains in weeks, not years. Modular (staking, governance, IBC, auth, bank…) — battle-tested by Osmosis, dYdX v4, Celestia, and 100+ chains.

properties.title: CometBFT (ex-Tendermint)
properties.desc: BFT engine renamed in 2023. Instant finality, ~1-second blocks, no forks. Known validator set per zone — secure as long as < 1/3 are Byzantine.

properties.title: App-Specific Sovereignty
properties.desc: Each chain tunes gas, governance, and upgrades to its own use case — no shared block space competition, no need to fit inside someone else's VM.

cosmos.atomBody: Hub security via staking · governance votes · Interchain Security lets opt-in chains rent the Hub validator set instead of bootstrapping their own.
cosmos.beyondBodyB: (2024+) extends IBC to Ethereum and other non-Cosmos chains — trust-minimised messaging, no centralised bridge.

cosmosEco.heading: Cosmos ecosystem — what runs across IBC
cosmosEco.subtitle: The IBC graph connects 110+ chains. Each one specialised — and the most-used app on Cosmos isn't on the Hub itself, it's on the zones.

xrp.heading: XRP Ledger — a purpose-built settlement rail
xrp.takeaway: XRPL is a purpose-built rail for payments, FX and tokenised real-world assets — fast and cheap by design. It is not a general-purpose smart-contract platform, and that trade-off is deliberate.

pillars.label: Native ops
pillars.title: DEX & payments are first-class
pillars.body: Order-book DEX has been in the protocol since 2012 (no smart contract); native AMM (XLS-30) joined in 2024. Optimised for these jobs — but the rule-set is fixed.

pillars.label: Federated validation
pillars.title: UNL — operators pick validators
pillars.body: Anyone can read and use the chain, but each node trusts a Unique Node List of validators (Federated Byzantine Agreement, ≥ 80% agree per round). Permissionless to use, federated to validate.

pillars.label: Cross-chain reach
pillars.title: One API to 50+ chains
pillars.body: Axelar GMP lets XRPL apps reach EVM, Cosmos, Sui and more — payment + message in a single call, with no bespoke bridge contract per pair.

xrp.designLabel: How it's built — and where the programmability lives

design.title: Fast & cheap by design
design.desc: ~1,500 tx/s in theory (a few hundred in practice), 3–5 s finality. A tiny XRP burn (~$0.0002/tx) makes spam uneconomic — and there is no fee-market spike.

design.title: Trust Lines / IOUs
design.desc: Issued tokens (RLUSD, stablecoins, RWA) live as balances on a Trust Line — a permission the holder grants the issuer. A different mental model from ERC-20.

design.title: Smart-contract logic lives off the base layer
design.desc: The XRPL mainnet has no general smart contracts — on purpose. Richer logic runs on separate chains: the XRPL EVM sidechain (Solidity, 2025) and Xahau, a sister network where 'Hooks' (small WASM snippets) execute. The base L1 stays deliberately simple.

design.title: Built for institutions
design.desc: RLUSD — an NYDFS-regulated stablecoin (live Dec 2024) settling on XRPL + Ethereum. RippleNet ODL uses XRP as a bridge currency, and CBDC pilots (Bhutan, Palau, Colombia) run on XRPL tech.

xrp.honestTitle: Honest context — what you give up
xrp.honestBody: A smaller smart-contract surface than the EVM, and validation that is federated: anyone can run a node, but the default validator set ships with the software. The bet is payments, RWA and cross-chain settlement — not general-purpose dApps.

xrpAnim.heading: XRPL ↔ Axelar — One API to Reach Every Chain
xrpAnim.subtitle: You just saw what XRPL is good at (payments, native DEX, RWA). Here's how it talks to the rest of the multi-chain world — without writing a bespoke bridge contract per pair.

quiz.question: Cross-chain bridges have been responsible for the largest hacks in crypto history — Ronin ($625M), Wormhole ($320M), Nomad ($190M). What architectural property makes bridges such high-value targets?
options: Bridges use proof-of-authority consensus controlled by a single company, making them easy to corrupt.
Bridges require KYC verification, creating a centralized identity database attackers can exploit.
Bridges concentrate large amounts of locked assets in a single smart contract on one chain while issuing representations on another — creating a honeypot with a single point of failure.
Bridges are slower than direct transactions, giving attackers more time to execute front-running attacks during the transfer window.
quiz.explanation: To bridge 1 ETH from Ethereum to another chain, you lock the ETH in a smart contract on Ethereum and mint a wrapped version on the destination chain. Every user who bridges concentrates their locked assets in that one contract — making it an increasingly valuable target. The Ronin bridge held $625M in locked ETH and USDC before attackers compromised 5 of 9 validator keys and drained it. The fundamental tension is that bridges require centralization (trusted validators or multisig) to operate efficiently, which directly conflicts with blockchain's trust minimization principle. Native interoperability protocols like IBC avoid this by design.

takeaways.title: Section 04 — Key Takeaways
items: Each chain is an island: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Fabric cannot read each other's ledgers — so value and messages need a route
Real needs drive it: cheaper L2 lanes, Bitcoin in DeFi, stablecoins on many chains, game assets, private data with public settlement
Three routes, one question — who do you trust? Bridges: an operator. IBC: the maths and both chains. Layer 0: one shared validator set
Bridges are the most hacked component in crypto (Ronin $625M, Wormhole $320M) — using one is a trust decision; prefer official bridges
XRP Ledger is a payments rail that reaches other chains through Axelar rather than a bespoke bridge per pair
